Thank you for the opportunity to speak today. I want to share an initiative that can
transform both healthcare education and continue to impact the lives of people in our community
which would be a dedicated space for a multi-disciplinary student-led clinic in the Saskatchewan
Field House. Neurological conditions such as stroke, traumatic brain injury, spinal cord injuries,
Parkinson's disease and multiple sclerosis affect thousands of individuals in the province and
in Saskatchewan. These conditions often require long-term coordinated care for occupational
therapists, physical therapists, and speech-language pathologists. Unfortunately, access to these
services is often limited by cost, insurance restrictions, and provider shortages. We envision a clinic
where occupational therapy, physiotherapy, and speech-language pathology students work together
under faculty and staff supervision to provide comprehensive, no-cost care to members of our community.
This clinic would serve two critical purposes. One, improve access for residents,
as many individuals with neurological conditions cannot afford ongoing therapy. This clinic ensures
that no one is left behind. Two, train future professionals. Students will gain hands-on experience
in a collaborative environment, learning to deliver patient-centered care as part of an interdisciplinary
team. The School of Rehabilitation Science has already proven that this model works.
Since the fall of 2024, we've run a pilot program called Neuromoves at the Saskatchewan Field House.
In partnership with the chronic disease management through the Saskatchewan Health Authority,
this program focuses on physical therapy for clients with complex neurological conditions,
and the results have been life-changing. Since the program began, the physiotherapy students
have been able to help around 40 community members. Some success stories include helping an
individual who had a spinal cord injury 20 years ago, stand with assistance for the first time.
Help a young woman with multiple sclerosis return to the workforce, and help a man who
had a stroke avoid needing long-term care and remain in his home. These success stories are only
the start of what could be accomplished if the spaces obtained that could also accommodate
other disciplines such as occupational therapy and speech-language pathology. In the fall of
2026, for the first time ever in the province, we will begin training students in occupational therapy
and speech-language pathology at the University of Saskatchewan. These students will join the
clinic, expanding services to include occupational therapy and speech-language pathology interventions.
In preparation for the expansion, the School of Rehabilitation Science has engaged with partners
at the University of Saskatchewan, and have unfortunately exhausted all other options on the
university campus for a space that needs the needs of these participants. The space at the
Field House would serve the needs of the expanded program and allow more services to be
provided to the community members well into the future. The proposed space would include
two private and one semi wheelchair accessible treatment rooms, a large open area for assessments
with the ceiling track and harness, a group programming room which is crucial for speech-language
pathology and a barrier-free reception area. These upgrades would allow us to offer more robust
well-rounded treatment options for the participants. The dedicated space means that we can continue
to provide accessible care for clients who might otherwise go without develop inter-professional
education opportunities through impactful, clinical placements which make up one third of the
student curriculum and continue to impact community members through improved quality of life,
functional independence and prevention of secondary complications. In closing, this is not just
a clinic space, it is a bridge between education and community health. It is an opportunity for
